anatomy.lede: A sea butterfly is a snail the size of a lentil, with a glassy shell and a foot turned into a pair of beating wings.

hotspots.label: Wing
hotspots.text: The wings are parapodia: flexible flaps that evolved from the snail's foot.

hotspots.label: Second wing
hotspots.text: During each stroke the wings clap together and fling apart, a 'clap and fling' trick also used by tiny flying insects.

hotspots.label: Shell
hotspots.text: The very thin shell coils to the left, with five to six whorls, and is made of aragonite, a form of calcium carbonate that dissolves easily in acidic water.

hotspots.label: Soft body
hotspots.text: The soft body, dark purple to violet in life, can pull right back inside the shell when the animal is disturbed.

stats.label: Share of polar zooplankton at times

body.lede: Moving through water at the scale of a few millimetres is neither quite swimming nor quite flying, and the sea butterfly does a little of both.

systems.title: Rowing and flying at once
systems.text: High-speed filming showed a complex three-dimensional wing-stroke with elements of both rowing and flapping flight, plus a rotation of the whole body. Smaller animals beat their wings faster than larger ones.

systems.title: Sawtooth climbs
systems.text: Swimming sea butterflies rise along a zigzag, sawtooth path as each stroke rocks the body. When they stop, they sink smoothly at 5–45 mm per second.

systems.title: A shell that thickens with depth
systems.text: In the Barents Sea, living sea butterflies had denser, larger and thicker shells the deeper they were caught, down to about 300 m.

survival.lede: Almost everything in polar seas eats sea butterflies, and their main defence is a shell that is itself under threat.

tactics.title: Retreat and drop the net
tactics.text: When disturbed, it pulls back into its shell and abandons its mucus feeding web.

tactics.title: Growing out of danger
tactics.text: One specialist predator, the sea angel Paedoclione doliiformis, eats only young sea butterflies with shells under 1 mm across.

threats.title: Corrosive coastal water
threats.text: Off Washington, Oregon and California in 2011, 53% of sea butterflies caught near shore and 24% offshore had severe shell dissolution. Researchers estimate such damage near shore has doubled since pre-industrial times and is on track to triple by 2050.

threats.title: Dissolving in the lab
threats.text: In week-long experiments with Puget Sound animals, shell damage rose steadily as the water's aragonite saturation fell, and survival was lowest in the most corrosive water.

life.lede: A sea butterfly lives fast, changing sex as it grows and completing its life within a year or two.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: Sperm is passed in packets called spermatophores, and eggs are laid in ribbon-like clusters, mostly in summer but some in winter.

stages.name: Veliger larva
stages.text: The eggs hatch into tiny swimming veliger larvae.

stages.name: Juvenile
stages.text: The smallest young, 0.2–0.4 mm across, live mainly in the top 50 m; larger animals range down to about 150 m.

stages.name: Male
stages.text: Every sea butterfly matures first as a male.

stages.name: Female
stages.text: Once larger than about 5 mm, it becomes female.
